title: ⭐ Practice: the words of a school, the words of a job

questions.prompt: A school-leaver has answered an advertisement, and the firm now calls him in to answer questions face to face about the post. Which stage of a job search has he reached?
questions.explanation: The interview is the stage at which the firm meets the candidate and questions him; the module places it after the right qualifications and training have been recognised. The application form is written and comes earlier, and it is filled in alone. The employment agency is one of the two ways of finding the advertisement in the first place. The wages are not a stage at all: they are one of the things the candidate asks about once he is in the room.

questions.prompt: A pupil cannot follow the lesson because he does not hear what the teacher says. Which of the nine labels of the module names his difficulty?
questions.explanation: An impairment names the faculty that is affected, and the faculty here is hearing. A speech impairment concerns producing speech, not receiving it, and the two are easy to swap because a pupil who has never heard clearly often speaks unclearly as well. A learning disability affects one particular operation such as reading or counting, whatever the pupil hears. A chronic health problem is an illness that keeps coming back, which is a medical fact rather than a difficulty with one sense.

questions.prompt: A primary school takes three children with disabilities into its ordinary classes instead of sending them to a separate institution. What does your module call that practice?
questions.explanation: Mainstreaming is precisely the practice of integrating children with disabilities into regular school programmes. Special education is the tempting answer and the wrong one: it is the whole field, and mainstreaming is one choice made inside it — a school that sent the same three children to a separate institution would still be doing special education. Defectology is another, older name for that same field, not for this particular practice. Distance learning belongs to the other half of the module and has nothing to do with disability.

questions.prompt: A secretary turns the question "Where does the candidate live?" into a note for the file. Her draft reads: "The manager wanted to know where did the candidate live." What must she change?

options.text: Keep did, and write lived instead of live.
Take out did, and leave live exactly as it stands.
Take out did, and write lived instead of live.
Take out where, and write if in its place.

questions.explanation: An indirect question takes the word order of a statement, so the auxiliary that built the direct question is not carried over at all: did goes. The tense then has to be carried by the verb itself, and since the reporting verb is in the past, the present live moves back to lived. The result is: the manager wanted to know where the candidate lived. Keeping did leaves the inversion in place, which is the commonest fault of the whole exercise. Taking did out and leaving live gives a verb with no tense and no agreement. And where must stay: if and whether replace nothing — they are what a question with no WH word takes instead.

questions.prompt: A part-time evening course takes six hours a week; the full-time day course takes twelve. Which sentence states the difference the way this module does?

options.text: The evening course takes half as long as the day course.
The evening course takes twice as long as the day course.
The evening course takes half as longer as the day course.
The evening course takes a half as long than the day course.

questions.explanation: Six hours against twelve is a scale of one to two, and the sentence is about the evening course, the smaller of the two, so the multiplier is half: half as long as. Twice as long reverses the two courses and describes the day course instead. Half as longer puts a comparative inside the block, where the adjective must stay in its base form. And a half as long than fails twice over: the multiplier is half, without an article, and the structure closes on as, never on than.

questions.prompt: A head teacher writes in her report: "The pupils ___ parents came to the meeting all improved during the term." Which word fills the gap?
questions.explanation: The clause says that the parents belong to those pupils, and the relative pronoun of possession is whose — it stands in the place of their. who would make the pupils themselves the subject of came, but the subject printed after the gap is parents. whom is the object form of who and would need a verb looking for an object. which is for things and animals, never for pupils.
